original_summary: Modern Art is a 3–5 player auction game. Players sell painting cards from hidden hands using several auction types, and an artist's value depends on how many of that artist's cards are played. The auctioneer's choice of which card to sell is the main lever on the market, and the richest player after four seasons wins.

review.evidence: In the previous variation the bid cap of 50 sat below the value of every top-two painting (60–100), so bidding 50 weakly dominated for every non-auctioneer. The fixed tie-break (earliest seat after the auctioneer) then decided who got every valuable painting, which handed seats 2, 3, 4 and 1 fixed rounds. No literal never-lose policy existed: always-50 loses to sensible play by overpaying for rank-4/5 cards, and always-0 never gains surplus. But allocation was decided by seat order, not by choices.

Market counts rose on every random draw regardless of play, so nobody could influence values. Under good play the outcome hinged on whether the deck put strong cards into your three tie-break rounds, a swing of about 90–150 points. A good player only gained by avoiding late overpays.

Once 'bid the cap on anything plausibly in the top two' is found, little remains to improve. The hot-artist bonus (+20, about +4 per painting on average) was too small to reward inference, and the four clues together revealed it exactly.

There was hidden information (deck order, hot artist), but it could only be estimated, not acted on. There was no plan to make, since nobody controlled which cards entered the market, and bluffing in talk changed little under a capped bid and a fixed tie-break. The original's real reasoning, choosing which card to sell and reading opponents' hands from their sales, was missing.
Money, market counts, ranks, painting values and scores are all arithmetic on tracked numbers. No judge is needed.
Turn-based sealed bids and text talk with no board. It sat within limits, though the attribute count had to be stated carefully.

problems: P1: Bid cap below painting value. A cap of 50 under top-painting values of 60–100 makes bidding the cap dominant and removes price discovery.
P2: Seat tie-break lottery. Ties at the cap went to the fixed seat after the auctioneer, so allocation of valuable paintings was decided by seat and deck order, not skill.
P3: No player control of the market. Counts rose on random draws, removing the original game's central lever (the auctioneer choosing which artist to push) and leaving nothing to plan.
P4: Weak and fully revealable hidden information. The hot bonus was small and the four clues jointly identified it, so inference and bluffing barely mattered.
P5: Last-auctioneer advantage. With a fixed start, the same seat always auctions round 12 with an almost fully known market, a built-in seat edge.
P6: Rank-5 values and the 80-point top value made weak paintings pure traps and the top artist a jackpot, amplifying luck.

changes.what: Deal all 20 cards out, 5 hidden cards to each player. Each round the auctioneer chooses which card from their own hand to put up for sale. Only auctioned cards raise market counts, and each player auctions exactly 3 of their 5 cards, so 8 cards never reach the market.
changes.why: This restores the original's core decision of which artist to push, and makes hidden hands the hidden state to infer: what others still hold and what they will play.

changes.what: Make bids any whole number from 0 up to the bidder's current money, with no fixed cap.
changes.why: Prices are found by bidding, and no cap sits below value. Whole-number bids make exact ties rare.

changes.what: Resolve ties among highest non-auctioneer bids by giving the painting to the tied player with the least current money. If they are still tied, the painting is discarded unsold and nobody pays, though the market count still rises.
changes.why: No seat is favoured, and a full tie benefits no one, which discourages tying on purpose.

changes.what: Replace the hot artist and its clues with hidden hands as the single strong hidden element. Talk is about holdings and intentions ('I am sitting on C, it will top the market').
changes.why: The hidden hand is the original game's real hidden information, and it drives both planning and bluffing. One strong hidden element is preferred over a weak extra one, and dropping the clues keeps the game inside the attribute limit.

changes.what: Draw the round-1 auctioneer at random at setup. Auctioneers then rotate clockwise, so each seat auctions exactly 3 times.
changes.why: The seat that makes the last, best-informed sale is no longer fixed. It is also no longer known before the game starts.

changes.what: Set painting values to 60 for an artist ranked 1st, 40 for 2nd, 20 for 3rd, and 0 for 4th and 5th, with starting money of 100. Rank ties are broken alphabetically, which is known in advance.
changes.why: This follows the original's top-three payout and narrows the top-artist jackpot. A known tie rule is something players can plan around rather than luck.

keeps: Auctioneer sells a card from a hidden hand; the buyer pays the auctioneer, or the bank if the auctioneer buys their own card.
Artist value is set by how many of that artist's cards were played, with the top three artists paying.
The sealed-bid auction type from the original.
If nobody bids, the auctioneer keeps the painting for free (the original open-auction rule).
The richest player at the end wins, counting money plus painting value.

recommendation.reason: Restoring hidden hands and the auctioneer's choice of card, removing the bid cap and making ties seat-neutral gives a buildable game. In it, market manipulation, reading opponents' hands and price judgement decide the winner.

variation.name: Modern Art: Private Collections
variation.summary: Four dealers each hold five hidden paintings. In turn each chooses one to sell by sealed bid, and the artists whose works reach the market most become valuable. Players push the artists they own, read opponents' holdings from what they sell and how they bid, and bluff in open talk.
variation.rules:
SETUP
- There are exactly 4 players, in seats 1 to 4.
- There are five artists: A, B, C, D and E. The deck has 20 cards, 4 of each artist.
- Shuffle the deck and deal 5 cards to each player. Each hand is private: only its owner sees it.
- Each player starts with 100 money. Money is public.
- Each artist has a MARKET COUNT, starting at 0. Market counts are public.
- Each player has a COLLECTION, starting empty. Collections are public.
- Draw one seat at random to be the auctioneer in round 1.

EACH ROUND (12 rounds)
1. OFFER. The auctioneer chooses one card from their own hand. It is removed from the hand and revealed as the painting for sale. That artist's market count rises by 1, whether or not the painting sells.
2. TALK. Every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. All four messages are then shown to everyone. Messages bind nobody, and players may lie.
3. BID. All 4 players, including the auctioneer, secretly and simultaneously choose a bid. A bid is any whole number from 0 up to the player's current money. A bid above the player's money counts as all of their money.
4. RESOLVE.
   a. If every bid is 0, the auctioneer keeps the painting for free.
   b. Otherwise the highest bid wins.
   c. The auctioneer wins only if their bid is strictly higher than every other bid. If the auctioneer wins, they pay their bid to the bank.
   d. If one non-auctioneer has the highest bid, that player wins and pays their bid to the auctioneer.
   e. If two or more non-auctioneers tie for the highest bid (and the auctioneer did not bid more), the tied player with the least current money wins and pays their bid to the auctioneer.
   f. If the tied players also have equal money, the painting is discarded unsold and nobody pays. The market count still keeps its +1.
   g. A won painting goes into the winner's collection and stays there to the end.
5. REVEAL. All four bids, the winner (if any) and the price paid are announced.
6. ROTATE. The auctioneer role passes clockwise to the next seat, so each seat is auctioneer in exactly 3 rounds.
- Each player auctions 3 of their 5 cards. Their remaining 2 cards are never played and never count.

END OF GAME (after round 12)
1. Rank the five artists by market count, highest first. Ties are broken alphabetically: A above B above C above D above E.
2. Each painting in a collection is worth: 60 if its artist ranks 1st, 40 if 2nd, 20 if 3rd, and 0 if 4th or 5th.
3. Each player's SCORE is their money plus the total value of their collection.
variation.objective: After round 12, the player with the highest score (money plus collection value) wins. If two or more players tie for the highest score, the game is a draw between them.
variation.expected_effect: Auctioneers choose sales that push artists they and their allies of the moment already own, or that starve a rival's collection. Buyers must estimate final ranks from public counts, their own hand and what others' choices reveal about their hands. They then bid up to their estimate of value, not to a cap, so price discovery decides who buys. Holding back cards (only 3 of 5 are played) creates planning over several rounds and bluffing. Talk passes both tests. Players disagree because the seller wants high prices while buyers want low ones, and each player wants the artists in their own collection and hand to rank top. A player who believes 'C will win, I hold three' may overpay for C when the speaker actually intends to sell D, so following a claim can lose. Thoughtless policies lose: always-0 gains no surplus and falls behind; always bidding all its money spends 100 on one painting worth at most 60; always selling a random card wastes the lever. Seat order no longer decides allocation, and the last auction belongs to a randomly drawn seat.

balanced.evidence:
PAINTING VALUES. Twelve of the 20 cards are drawn, and market counts sum to 12. A drawn card is more likely to belong to a high-count artist, so the expected value of a sold painting is sum(count_i × value_i) / 12. Examples: counts 4,3,2,2,1 give (320+180+80+40+0)/12 = 51.7; counts 4,4,2,1,1 give (320+240+40+20+0)/12 = 51.7; counts 3,3,2,2,2 give (240+180+80+40+0)/12 = 45. The hot bonus adds 20 × E[hot count]/12 = 20 × 2.4/12 ≈ +4. So the average painting is worth about 50–56. Cards of the 1st and 2nd ranked artists are worth 60–100. The bid cap is 50, so it sits below the value of every top-two painting.

DECISION TABLE (non-auctioneer, late round, painting known to be rank 1, worth 80 or 100 if hot). Surplus if you win at bid b is V − b:
- b=50: surplus 30/50. Wins unless an earlier-seated player also bids 50.
- b=40: surplus 40/60, but only if nobody bids 50, which never happens among competent players.
- b=0–30: surplus 50–80/70–100, same condition.
Every bid up to 50 is profitable, so 50 weakly dominates for every non-auctioneer, and all competent players bid 50. The auctioneer cannot win a tie, so their own bid is irrelevant.

The winner of every valuable painting is therefore fixed by the tie-break: the seat immediately clockwise of the auctioneer.
- Seat 2 takes rounds 1, 5, 9.
- Seat 3 takes rounds 2, 6, 10.
- Seat 4 takes rounds 3, 7, 11.
- Seat 1 takes rounds 4, 8, 12, including round 12, when the market is almost fully known.
This is an information edge from move order. It also turns auctions into a seat lottery.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule):
- Always 50 vs three sensible players: it wins every painting the others value below 50 and pays 50 for rank-4 or rank-5 cards worth 20/0, losing 30–50 each time. It runs out of money and usually loses. It is not a never-lose policy.
- Always 50 vs random players (each bids 50 with probability 1/6): it wins most auctions at about breakeven value, so it usually beats random.
- Always 0: it never buys and gains only auctioneer income. It loses to sensible play.

No literal never-lose policy exists. The real problem is the near-dominant 'bid the cap on anything plausibly worth more than 50', with the seat tie-break deciding allocation. The original game's price discovery is gone. Players also cannot influence market counts at all: counts rise on every draw regardless of play. That removes the original game's main lever.

playable.evidence:
The rules cover every case.
- An all-zero round discards the painting with a 10 penalty to the auctioneer.
- Ties among non-auctioneers go to the earliest seat after the auctioneer. The auctioneer needs a strictly highest bid to win.
- Over-money bids are clamped, and all amounts stay multiples of 10.
- Unsold cards still count toward the market.
- The end ranking includes zero-count artists, with an alphabetical tie-break.

The game is finite at 12 rounds and is scored by arithmetic on kept numbers.

Limits:
- steps_per_round 11 ≤ 20.
- choice_steps 2 ≤ 4.
- Random draws per round: 1 (the deck pop). The hot draw and clue deal happen at setup.
- Hidden elements: deck order, hot artist, private clues. That is 3, which is within the limit; the designer's figure of 2 undercounts.
- Attributes: this is feasible only if each collection is a list attribute. Count 5 market counts + 4 money + 4 collection lists + hot + 4 clues + deck + auctioneer = 20, which is at the limit, not 17. Per-artist holdings as separate attributes (20) would exceed the cap.
- The end ranking needs the arithmetic_ranking workaround (calc steps at game end).

Talk is simultaneous. It suits four players with competing interests, who also hold clues they can share truthfully or falsely about the hot artist. The game uses no board, clock or judge.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Artist values come entirely from the random deck order. No player choice changes any market count, so there is nothing to plan or manipulate, only to estimate.

All-good-play outcome: everyone bids 50 on rank-1/2 cards and lower on weak ones. Each top painting goes to the deterministic tie-break seat. Each player's surplus is then decided by whether the random draw put valuable cards in that player's 3 tie-break rounds. With 12 draws and roughly 5–7 high-value cards, the spread is large. One seat can easily receive 3 top cards while another receives 0, a swing of about 90–150 points. That is far larger than anything inference adds.

The inference element is the hot artist. It is worth only +20 per card, about +4 per painting on average. All four clues together identify it exactly, so talk either reveals it or is distrusted, and the stakes are small either way. Bluffing in talk changes little because bids are capped and the tie-break is fixed.

Estimate: well over half of the result is chance (deck order relative to seat rotation). A good reasoner is only modestly favoured, through avoiding overpaying for weak artists late.

required_changes: Give players influence over values: deal each player a hidden hand of cards and let the auctioneer choose which card to sell each round. Only cards actually auctioned should raise the market count, as in the original.
Raise the bid range above typical painting value, for example 0–120 in steps of 10, so that price discovery decides who wins and the bid cap does not.

Replace the fixed seat tie-break so that it does not hand top paintings to a predetermined seat. For example, when non-auctioneers tie for highest, no one buys and the auctioneer must take the card at the tied price, or award ties to the tied player with the lowest current money.

Make the hidden information matter more: raise the hot bonus to 40 or more, and give clues that do not jointly reveal the hot artist (for example two players share a clue and one artist is never named). Inference and deception in talk then carry real weight.
State the attribute plan explicitly, with collections as per-player lists, and correct the declared counts to attributes 20 and hidden_elements 3.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFF SCALE. 12 of the 20 cards are offered, each artist at most 4. A typical spread is 4/3/3/1/1. Painting value is then about 4x60 + 3x40 + 3x20 = 420, set against 400 starting money, so paintings matter as much as cash. Money only changes hands between players, except when an auctioneer buys their own card and pays the bank.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule).
(1) ALWAYS BID 0. The player never collects paintings. As auctioneer they set no reserve, so the other three can shade their bids. With three rival bidders, first-price competition keeps prices near value minus a margin. The zero-bidder banks less than full value on 3 sales. A buyer who gets a 60-value painting for, say, 40 is ahead by 20 per purchase on top of their own sale income. Against sensible play: loses. Against random bidders (uniform 0..money): random bidders overpay often, so the zero-bidder can win some games, but not almost every time. Against all-in bidders: wins, since they bankrupt themselves.
(2) ALWAYS BID ALL MONEY. Pays 100 for the round-1 card, whose maximum worth is 60. Then has 0 money and cannot compete. Loses to sensible play and to the zero-bidder.
(3) ALWAYS BID A FIXED VALUE, e.g. 30. Sensible players outbid it on cards worth 40-60 and let it overpay on cards that end up worth 0. Loses.
No bid level is strictly better whatever the others do: the right bid depends on the expected final rank and on rival bids. So this is a real first-price auction with an endogenous value.

SEATS. The starting auctioneer is random, and each seat auctions exactly 3 times. The round-12 auctioneer's choice can tip the final ranking: a +1 can swap 3rd and 4th, worth 20 per painting held. But the card is offered before the bids, so it is priced in. Rivals can see the public counts and collections and anticipate it. The earliest auctioneer sells under the most uncertainty, but buyers face the same uncertainty. The edge is modest and comes from planning, not structure.

The alphabetical tie-break gives a known, symmetric bias toward A that everyone can price in. Every seat can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
The game is finite: 12 rounds. Bids, money, market counts and collections are all kept numbers. The ranking and scoring are arithmetic and need no judge, board or clock.

Limits against the stated complexity:
- steps_per_round 13 (limit 20)
- choice_steps_per_round 3 (limit 4): offer, talk, bid
- attributes 19 (limit 20): money x4, hand x4, collection x4, market x5, auctioneer, price
- hidden_elements 1 (limit 3): hands
- random draws: setup only, 0 per round (limit 1)
- rounds 12 (limit 40)

Workarounds needed:
- The least-money tie-break uses the player_attribute_compare workaround.
- The final rank uses arithmetic_ranking with calc.
- Removing a card from a hand is a list remove.
All of these are supported.

The bid is a simultaneous poll, which is correct. Talk is simultaneous and justified with 4 players. Players disagree about which artists should rise because their hidden hands and public collections differ. Following a proposal, such as 'let's all push C', can cost you if the speaker holds C. Messages also give hints about hands to reason about.

One minor gap: a tie between the auctioneer and exactly one non-auctioneer. Rule c (auctioneer needs strictly higher) together with rule d reads naturally as the non-auctioneer winning, so it is resolvable.

This is not a fixed-length cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE. The deal decides which artists each player can push. That is real luck, but each player chooses 3 of their 5 cards, and every card is priced by bidding. A player dealt a strong hand still has to buy paintings at a sensible price. I estimate chance at about 25-35% of the result.

WHAT CAN BE INFERRED.
- Rivals' hands: all 20 cards are dealt and each player sees their own 5, so they know 5 of every 20. Offers so far and talk narrow down what others hold.
- Final ranking: estimated from public counts plus the inferred hands.
- Rival bid levels: revealed every round, which allows opponent modelling for the next sealed bid.

WAYS TO ACT ON IT.
- Which card to offer, which also moves the ranking.
- How much to bid.
- Whether to bid on your own card as a reserve, which costs you money paid to the bank.

IF ALL PLAY WELL. Sensible bidders converge on shaded expected values. The winner then depends on better forecasting of the ranking and better timing of purchases, not on a single random draw. A strong reasoner is clearly favoured over a naive bidder.
